title: Aachen housing
description: Why rents in Aachen rose: students and other households competing for flats that take years to build, on land the city designates slowly. Model years run from 2000 to 2040; rents are in 2000 prices.

landDesignated.label: New land / year
landDesignated.unit: dwellings’ worth of land per year

rentChange.label: Rent change
rentChange.equation: rent * max(0, rentGrowth) + (rent - rentFloor) * min(0, rentGrowth)

otherHouseholds.label: Non-student households
otherHouseholds.description: Non-student households wanting a flat here

otherDemand.label: Non-student households with a flat
otherDemand.description: Households with a flat of their own

wanted.label: Households wanting a flat at the starting rent

notionalVacancy.label: Vacancy if all housed
notionalVacancy.description: Vacancy if everyone had a flat

baseIntake.label: BASE_INTAKE
baseIntake.meaning: Intake that keeps the student number constant

studentsPerFlat.label: STUDENTS_PER_FLAT
studentsPerFlat.meaning: Students per market flat: about half live in their own flat, half in flat shares

shareWithParents.label: SHARE_WITH_PARENTS
shareWithParents.meaning: Students in Aachen who live with their parents

hallPlaces.label: HALL_PLACES
hallPlaces.meaning: Places in student halls; the halls fill first

baseStudentsInTown.label: baseStudentsInTown
baseStudentsInTown.meaning: Students living in Aachen at the start

baseStudentDemand.label: BASE_STUDENT_DEMAND
baseStudentDemand.meaning: Market flats wanted by students at the start
baseStudentDemand.derived: (baseStudentsInTown - baseStudentsInTown * shareWithParents - min(baseStudentsInTown - baseStudentsInTown * shareWithParents, hallPlaces)) / studentsPerFlat

baseHouseholdSize.label: BASE_HOUSEHOLD_SIZE
baseHouseholdSize.meaning: People per non-student household at the start

baseOtherHouseholds.label: OTHER_HOUSEHOLDS
baseOtherHouseholds.meaning: Non-student households wanting a flat of their own at the start

normalVacancy.label: NORMAL_VACANCY
normalVacancy.meaning: Vacancy at which rents are stable

minVacancy.label: MIN_VACANCY
minVacancy.meaning: Flats always empty between tenants: about a month every eight years

baseShareOutside.label: BASE_SHARE_OUTSIDE
baseShareOutside.meaning: Share of students living outside at the start

maxShareOutside.label: MAX_SHARE_OUTSIDE
maxShareOutside.meaning: Ceiling set by bus and train capacity

spilloverElasticity.label: SPILLOVER_ELASTICITY
spilloverElasticity.meaning: Rent +10% moves the indicated share up 21% (1.1²)

householdRentElasticity.label: HOUSEHOLD_RENT_ELASTICITY
householdRentElasticity.meaning: Rent +10% means about 2.4% fewer non-student households want a flat of their own here

baseFlats.label: BASE_FLATS
baseFlats.meaning: Flats at the start: exactly 3% empty

growthResponse.label: GROWTH_RESPONSE
growthResponse.meaning: Share of the demand growth builders expect that they build for; 0 knocks the link out

normalPipeline.label: NORMAL_PIPELINE
normalPipeline.meaning: Flats in planning and construction when starts are normal

pipelineResponse.label: pipelineResponse
pipelineResponse.meaning: How strongly developers hold back when the pipeline is fuller than normal. 0, the default, means they ignore it: B5 is off in the model as drawn; 1 switches it on.

baseRent.label: BASE_RENT
baseRent.meaning: Rent at the start, per m² per month

rentSensitivity.label: RENT_SENSITIVITY
rentSensitivity.meaning: Rent change per year when pressure = 1 (no empty flats)

maxRentFall.label: MAX_RENT_FALL
maxRentFall.meaning: Fastest rent can fall per year

maxRentRise.label: MAX_RENT_RISE
maxRentRise.meaning: Fastest rent can rise per year

rentFloor.label: RENT_FLOOR
rentFloor.meaning: Rent at which letting stops paying: falls slow down towards it

landYears.label: LAND_YEARS
landYears.meaning: Buildable land at the start, in years of normal building

baseLand.label: BASE_LAND
baseLand.meaning: Buildable land at the start, in flats

landUseTime.label: LAND_USE_TIME
landUseTime.meaning: Shortest time in which the remaining land can be used up

landPriceElasticity.label: LAND_PRICE_ELASTICITY
landPriceElasticity.meaning: Half as much land doubles its price

policyResponse.label: POLICY_RESPONSE
policyResponse.meaning: Subsidised starts per unit of perceived pressure, as a share of typical starts

typicalStarts.label: TYPICAL_STARTS
typicalStarts.meaning: Flats Aachen completed per year on average, 2000–2024 (IT.NRW)

initialTrend.label: initialTrend
initialTrend.meaning: Yearly growth in non-student households the inputs start with. Builders already see it, and the flats they started for it in the years before are in the pipeline.

initialStarts.label: initialStarts
initialStarts.meaning: Starts per year in the years before the run

delay.shape: Second order: two stages of D / 2. Completions spread out and peak about D / 2 after the starts.
First order: each year closes 1 / MOVING_TIME of the remaining gap.
First order: each year closes 1 / POLICY_DELAY of the remaining gap.
Each year 1 / STUDY_YEARS of all students leave. Changing it also changes BASE_INTAKE, so the model still starts in balance.
Each year 1 / FLAT_LIFETIME of all flats are demolished. Changing it also changes NORMAL_STARTS and BASE_LAND.
First order: builders' count closes 1 / FORECAST_TIME of the gap each year, so the gap measures the growth they expect.

real.label: Aachen as recorded, then forecast
real.question: Students, non-student population and household size as recorded until 2025, then as official forecasts expect.

derivedFrom.method: Made by realInputs() in aachen-housing-loops/src/inputs.ts. Intake: the yearly arrivals that make the model's student stock follow the recorded student count (IT.NRW, continued by the city's figures), then the stock the medium first-year forecast builds. Population: the city's register from 2011, extended backwards by IT.NRW's growth rates, minus the 66% of students registered as residents, then the medium forecast. Household size: non-student population over households net of student households, with the register's trend before 2011 and IT.NRW's forecast after. Land: as many flats a year as were completed on average since 2000. Each curve is divided by its 2000 value.

balanced.label: Balanced
balanced.question: Does the model stay put when nothing changes? Every stock should hold its starting value.

no-new-students.label: No new students
no-new-students.question: Extreme condition: the universities stop admitting anyone in 2012.
no-new-students.expectation: Flats empty out and rents fall towards the level where letting stops paying.

student-flood.label: Student flood
student-flood.question: Extreme condition: three times the usual number of new students for five years from 2012, then back to normal.
student-flood.expectation: Students double to about 70,000 by 2017 and are back near 34,000 by the mid-2030s. Rents jump, the share living outside hits its 35% ceiling and building land runs out. When the extra students leave, flats built for them stand empty and rents fall below where they started.

no-new-land.label: No new building land
no-new-land.question: Extreme condition: from 2012 the city designates no more building land, everything else as recorded.
no-new-land.expectation: The land already designated is used up within a few years and building stops. Rents climb well above the recorded run and keep climbing as long as non-student households keep growing.

real-instant.label: Real data, no delays
real-instant.question: Equilibrium test: building, moving out, political recognition and builders spotting growth take months instead of years.
real-instant.expectation: Rent rises less and more smoothly, because flats arrive as soon as demand grows. The difference is largest in 2011–2015, when students arrived fastest.

real-half-step.label: Real data, half the time step
real-half-step.question: Integration error test: does halving the time step change the result?

supply.label: B1
supply.name: Supply response
supply.story: Low vacancy pushes rents up, building pays off, and new flats arrive years later.

spillover.label: B2
spillover.name: Priced out
spillover.story: High rents push students to Herzogenrath, Stolberg or Eschweiler, and make other households share, stay with their parents or live further out.

land.label: B3
land.name: Land scarcity
land.story: Every project uses up land. Scarce land gets expensive and makes the next project less profitable; without land nothing can be built.

policy.label: B4
policy.name: Political response
policy.story: A visible shortage leads, years later, to subsidised flats and student halls built regardless of profit.

pipeline.label: B5
pipeline.name: Pipeline awareness
pipeline.story: Developers count the flats already being planned and built, and start fewer when the pipeline is full. Off by default: the market as drawn ignores it.

links.intake→students: Each year a new cohort enrols. Students stay for the time at university, so the stock reacts slowly to a change in intake.
links.students→demand: Students who live in Aachen need somewhere to live. Some stay with their parents and some get a place in a hall; the rest rent on the market, on average 1.8 to a flat.
links.otherHouseholds→demand: Workers, families and retirees who would like a flat of their own in Aachen at the starting rent: the non-student population divided by the household size. Both are drawn over time in the controls.
links.students→demandGrowth: Builders watch how fast the number of households wanting a flat grows, students included, and notice a change in that growth only after a few years.
links.otherHouseholds→demandGrowth: Growth in non-student households counts the same way. A city that has been growing for years keeps building for growth.
links.demandGrowth→starts: On top of what pays off at today's rent, developers start as many flats a year as they expect new households, if there is land for them.
links.rent→demand: Higher rents make some households share a flat, stay with their parents or move further out: rent +10% means about 3% fewer of them want a flat of their own.
links.shareOutside→demand: Students who live in nearby towns don't need a flat in Aachen.
links.demand→notionalVacancy: More demand for the same number of flats means fewer empty flats.
links.flats→notionalVacancy: More flats for the same demand means more empty flats.
links.notionalVacancy→rent: When few flats are empty, or more households want one than there are flats, landlords raise rents. Rent is a stock: it keeps climbing for as long as the market is tighter than the normal 3% vacancy.
links.rent→profitability: Higher rents make new buildings worth more, so projects pay off.
links.profitability→starts: Developers start more projects when building pays off. They look at today's rents, not at the flats already in the pipeline, unless B5 is switched on.
links.starts→permitted: New projects enter planning and permitting.
links.permitted→underConstruction: After planning, building begins. Each of the two stages takes half of the construction delay.
links.underConstruction→flats: Flats are finished after the second half of the construction delay. Meanwhile vacancy stays low and developers keep starting more.
links.rent→shareOutside: Higher rents gradually push students to cheaper nearby towns. Bus and train capacity caps this at 35% of students.
links.starts→buildableLand: Each project uses up buildable land. The city designates new land in steady yearly amounts.
links.buildableLand→starts: Starts can't use up the remaining land faster than in LAND_USE_TIME years. No land, no building.
links.landDesignated→buildableLand: The city designates new building land. Drawn over time in the controls; 100% replaces what normal building uses up. With real data, land for as many flats as were completed each year on average.
links.buildableLand→landPrice: The scarcer buildable land gets, the more it costs.
links.landPrice→profitability: Land is about 30% of building costs, so dearer land makes projects less profitable.
links.notionalVacancy→perceivedPressure: A shortage turns into political pressure only after it has been visible for a few years.
links.perceivedPressure→subsidisedStarts: Pressure leads to funding for subsidised flats and student halls, built whether or not they are profitable.
links.subsidisedStarts→starts: Subsidised projects go through the same planning and construction stages.
links.permitted→starts: With B5 on, developers see the flats already in planning and start fewer when the pipeline is fuller than normal.
links.underConstruction→starts: With B5 on, flats under construction count as future supply too.
